title: Time for Space
blurb: Big O isn't only about time — it's also the EXTRA memory an algorithm uses beyond its input. Sort each approach by how much extra space it needs. This is the 'trade memory for speed' dimension interviewers love.

glossary.O(1) extra space: A fixed amount of extra memory no matter the input size — a few variables, counters, or pointers. These are the 'in-place' algorithms.
glossary.O(n) extra space: Extra memory that grows with the input — a hash set, dictionary, or stack that can end up holding as many items as the input.

levels.title: L1 · How much extra memory?
levels.prompt: Classify each approach by the EXTRA space it uses (ignore the input itself).
levels.hint: Which of these can grow to hold as many items as the input, and which keep just a few variables?

items.label: Contains Duplicate with a HashSet
items.note: adds each element to a set

levels.explain: Extra space is the memory used beyond the input. A HashSet or Dictionary can grow to hold up to n items → O(n), while two pointers or a single XOR accumulator use a fixed few variables → O(1).

failStates.title: A HashSet can hold everything
failStates.explain: In the worst case the set stores all n elements → O(n) extra space. That memory is exactly what you 'spend' to get O(1) lookups and O(n) time.

failStates.title: Two pointers are just two ints
failStates.explain: No matter how long the string, you only ever hold two index variables → O(1) extra space. That's the appeal of the two-pointer pattern.

failStates.title: XOR keeps a single number
failStates.explain: The whole trick is one accumulator → O(1) extra space, even though it visits all n elements (O(n) time).

levels.title: L2 · In-place or not?
levels.prompt: Same idea, a few more. Which need memory that grows with n?
levels.hint: Does it allocate something that scales with n, or does it work in place?

items.label: Reverse an array by swapping ends
Count word frequencies into a Dictionary

levels.explain: In-place work is O(1): Boyer-Moore keeps a candidate + counter, and reversing swaps ends with a temp variable. Anything that can grow with the input — a stack of brackets, a frequency dictionary — is O(n).

failStates.title: Boyer-Moore is O(1) space
failStates.explain: It keeps only a candidate and a counter — O(1) extra space. That's what makes it beat the hash-map / sorting approaches on memory.

failStates.title: The stack can grow to n
failStates.explain: For a string of all opening brackets, the stack holds all n of them before anything is popped → O(n) extra space.

failStates.title: Swapping in place is O(1)
failStates.explain: Reversing by swapping the ends toward the middle uses just a temp variable and two indices — O(1) extra space. No second array is allocated.
